newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power flat to slightly weaker.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power flat to slightly weaker.

text.p: Spot power prices in the U.S. West were flat to slightly lower amid cooler temperatures, market sources said Friday.
"Our temperatures are dropping and generation resources are really good," said an Arizona utility trade source. "By next week we will be capacity fat."

Cooler weather translates into lower demand in the Southwest, where usage peaks during the summer, but electricity is a key heating source in the Northwest, where winter temperatures are also beginning to kick in.
Market sources noted, however, that higher demand in the Northwest is having little spill-over impact in the Southwest due to constraints on interstate transmission lines.
Although recent maintenance work on the lines is due to end Sunday, they are indefinitely capped at 65 percent of capacity as studies into voltage support continue.
Firm power for peak-demand hours on Monday at the Palo Verde substation in Arizona was last quoted at $17.00-18.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), down from around $20.00 on Thursday.
Next-day spot quotes for firm, peak deliveries at the California-Oregon border (COB) were unchanged at $19.25-19.50 per MWh.
Monday Mid-Columbia peak quotes were $17.00-17.50, down from $17.50-18.00.
